paraphrase: The world, spoken of as 'he, she and it', undergoes origination, maintenance and dissolution; therefore it has an agent. It resolves into Hara and, because of mala, comes forth again from him; hence the learned say that he who is its end is also its beginning.

The Lord is one with souls and yet other than them (like the soul with the body, the vowel with the consonants); by his command (āṇai, his power) he stands inseparably with them and makes them come and go through births according to their twofold deeds (iruviṉai).

There is a soul within the body distinct from it: it denies that it is this or that ('not this'), it says 'my body', it knows through the five senses, it knows in dream, it does not experience in deep sleep, it is awakened, and it knows only when made to know.
notes: The list of the soul's marks is summarized from memory; the exact enumeration should be checked against the text.

paraphrase: The soul is not one of the inner organs (antaḥkaraṇa); bound by its innate mala it cannot know by itself, and it knows through the inner organs as a king through his ministers; it passes through the five states (avasthā).
The senses know their objects only through the soul yet do not know the soul; the soul likewise knows only through Śiva, who moves it as a magnet moves iron while himself remaining unchanged.
What is known by the senses is changing and perishing (acat); what cannot be known at all would be non-existent; the Real (Śiva) is neither — it is known by the soul through grace, not as an object.
Before the Real, the unreal does not appear; the unreal cannot know the Real; the soul, which knows both, is neither — it is sadasat (cat-acat), taking on the nature of whatever it is joined to.

To the soul that has done penance in former lives, the Lord comes as the guru and teaches: 'You have lived among the five senses like a prince brought up among hunters'; the soul then leaves them, knows it is not other than the Lord, and reaches his feet.

Seeing Śiva in one's own soul with the eye of knowledge given by grace, knowing the senses' world as a mirage (pēyttēr), taking refuge in the Lord's shade, and meditating on the five letters as prescribed, the soul is purified.
As the Lord is one with the soul, so the soul becoming one with him, acting only as his servant, is no longer touched by mala, māyā and the two deeds.
As the soul makes the eye see and itself sees, so Śiva makes the soul know and himself knows; by unforgetting love the soul reaches his feet.
Having washed away the three malas that hide the Lord's feet, the freed soul should join the true devotees and worship their holy garb and the temple as the Lord himself.
The Sanskrit first verse argues from the world's threefold character and its three functions that it has a maker, into whom it is withdrawn and from whom it comes forth again.
notes: Parallel of Civañāṉa Pōtam 1; wording not checked.

paraphrase: The opponents' section sets out in their own terms and then refutes the Lokāyata, the four Buddhist schools, the Jains, the Ājīvikas, the Mīmāṃsakas, the grammarians' word-Brahman, Māyāvāda Vedānta, Bhāskara's view, the Pāñcarātra, the Sāṃkhya and others, as a preparation for the Siddhānta.
notes: Fourteen schools are traditionally counted; the list here is partial and moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The Lord performs the five acts — creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment and grace — not for himself but out of compassion, so that souls may exhaust their karma and ripen their mala; even destruction is rest for the souls.
notes: Chapter-level reference; exact verse not given.

paraphrase: God's non-duality with souls means not identity but inseparability: he is one with them, different from them and together with them, as the vowel is in the consonants; the Vedic sayings of oneness are to be understood so.
notes: Chapter-level reference.

paraphrase: When the two deeds come into balance and the soul's mala has ripened, Śiva's power descends (catti nipātam) in four grades — very mild, mild, intense and very intense — fitting the soul for caryā, kriyā, yoga or jñāna; Śiva then comes as the guru and initiates.
notes: Chapter-level reference; the grade-to-path mapping is moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The guru initiates in seven ways — by look, touch, word, thought, instruction in the scriptures, yoga, and the fire rite (auttiri) — destroying the accumulated karma; the prārabdha that formed the body is exhausted by experience.
notes: The list of seven kinds is recalled at moderate-low confidence.

paraphrase: Caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna are four steps; the first three give the lower liberations (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya) and ripen the soul; only jñāna, given by the guru's grace, leads to union (sāyujya). Jñāna itself proceeds by hearing, reflection, clarity and abiding (kēṭṭal, cintittal, teḷital, niṭṭai).
In liberation the soul does not become Śiva nor perish; it abides inseparable from him, enjoying his bliss, as the malas, which are eternal, lie powerless.
notes: Chapter-level reference.

paraphrase: In question and answer with his guru Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti asks how the soul, pure by nature, came to be bound, why mala clings to it, and how grace works; the answers teach that āṇava is beginningless and that only the guru's grace releases the soul.

The dance of the Lord is the five acts: creation from the drum, protection from the hand that grants fearlessness, destruction from the fire, concealment from the planted foot, and release (grace) from the raised foot.
notes: Verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: In the five letters na-ma-śi-vā-ya, 'na' is concealment (tirōtam), 'ma' is mala, 'śi' is Śiva, 'vā' is his grace (aruḷ) and 'ya' is the soul; the soul standing between mala and Śiva should turn toward grace; placing 'śi' first (śivāya nama) is the subtle form.
notes: Section-level reference; the letter correspondences are recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The body and world are made of thirty-six tattvas: twenty-four of the soul (ātma-tattva: the elements, subtle elements, organs and inner organs), seven of knowledge (vidyā-tattva: māyā, kalā, kāla, niyati, vidyā, rāga, puruṣa) and five of Śiva (śiva-tattva); the soul must know them as not itself.
notes: Section-level reference.

paraphrase: The ten acts (tacakāriyam): seeing the form of the tattvas, seeing that they are insentient, purifying oneself of them; seeing the form of the soul, seeing the soul, purifying the soul; seeing the form of Śiva, seeing Śiva, union with Śiva (śiva-yoga) and enjoyment of Śiva (śiva-bhoga).
As the vowel 'a' pervades all letters, the Lord, without equal, pervades everything as knowledge.

original.text: அகர உயிர்போல் அறிவாகி எங்கும் நிகரில் இறைநிற்கும் நிறைந்து

paraphrase: The chapter on the dark mala (iruḷ-mala-nilai): āṇava is one, beginningless and hides the soul's knowledge as darkness hides objects — but, unlike darkness, it hides itself as well; it is removed not by the soul's effort but by grace.
notes: Chapter-level reference.

paraphrase: The chapter on grace (aruḷatu-nilai): grace is always present with the soul, as the sun's light is to the eye, yet the soul does not see it while covered by mala; grace is Śiva's own power.
notes: Chapter-level reference; the sun image is recalled at moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The chapter on grace embodied (aruḷ-uru-nilai): as a deer is caught with a decoy deer, Śiva takes human form as the guru to catch souls who know only human forms.
notes: Chapter-level; the decoy image is recalled at moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The chapter on the five letters (aintheḻuttu-aruḷ-nilai): the right order of the five letters places grace between Śiva and the soul, and meditating them so leads the soul to Śiva.
notes: Chapter-level reference.

paraphrase: The chapter on those who have attained (aṇaintōr taṉmai): the freed live without 'I' and 'mine', their acts are Śiva's acts, and they neither seek nor reject.
notes: Chapter-level reference.

paraphrase: The whole system in a hundred verses: the guru's lineage; the three padārthas; the soul's three states (kēvala, sakala, śuddha); the malas; the tattvas; grace, the guru and the means; and the bliss of release.

Umāpati refutes nine neighbouring views of soul, bonds and release — among them that the freed soul becomes equal to Śiva in every respect (Śivasamavāda), that the soul passes over into Śiva (Saṅkrāntavāda), that bonds remain like stone (Pāṣāṇavāda) — and upholds inseparable union in which the soul enjoys Śiva's bliss.
notes: Locator is a placeholder range for the whole work; the characterizations of the nine views are low confidence.

paraphrase: Grace alone brings the soul to Śiva; the guru's glance destroys the bonds; the one who knows by grace becomes one with Śiva without losing himself, and should remain in stillness.
Expanding the Tiruvuntiyār, it teaches the dissolution of the sense of 'I' in grace, the guru as Śiva, and the conduct of the jīvanmukta who acts without attachment.
Four verses on the meaning of raising Śiva's flag: the soul's bonds are cut and grace is proclaimed; tradition says the stuck festival flag at Chidambaram rose as they were sung.
Civañāṉa Muṉivar explains 'advaita' in the Civañāṉa Pōtam as 'non-separateness' (ananya), not numerical identity, and argues against the Māyāvādin reading of the Upaniṣadic identity sayings.
The ignorant say love and Śiva are two; none knows that love itself is Śiva; when they know that love is Śiva, they abide as love, as Śiva.

original.text: அன்பும் சிவமும் இரண்டென்பர் அறிவிலார் அன்பே சிவமாவது ஆரும் அறிகிலார் அன்பே சிவமாவது ஆரும் அறிந்தபின் அன்பே சிவமாய் அமர்ந்திருந் தாரே

paraphrase: Mankind is one family and God is one; think only good; there is no death (Yama) to fear; there is no other refuge — abide steadily in the mind and be saved.
notes: Opening line 'oṉṟē kulamum oruvaṉē tēvaṉum' ('one family, one God') is certain; verse number and the rest of the paraphrase moderate confidence.

paraphrase: If the body perishes the life-breath perishes and firm true knowledge cannot be reached; knowing the means to nourish the body, I nourished the body and so nourished the soul.
notes: Opening 'uṭampār aḻiyil uyirār aḻivar'; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: For the bountiful Lord the heart is the sanctum, the fleshly body the temple, the mouth the tower-gate; to those who have understood, the soul is the Śiva-liṅga, and the five deceiving senses are the lamps.
notes: Opening 'uḷḷam peruṅkōyil ūṉuṭampu ālayam'; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: May the world obtain the bliss that I have obtained.
notes: 'yāṉ peṟṟa iṉpam peṟuka ivvaiyakam'; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The Āgamas I received are nine: Kāraṇam, Kāmikam, Vīram, Cintam, Vātuḷam, Yāmaḷam, Kālōttaram, Cuppiram and Makuṭam.
notes: The list of nine Āgamas is recalled with moderate confidence; the verse number is low confidence.

paraphrase: The Veda and the Āgama are both true, both the Lord's scripture; one is general, the other special.
notes: Content moderate confidence; verse number low confidence.

paraphrase: The fifth tantra distinguishes the Śaiva schools (pure, impure, 'path', and severe-pure Śaiva) and teaches the four paths — caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna — each containing the others in miniature, leading to the worlds, nearness, form and union with Śiva.
notes: Tantra-level reference.

paraphrase: The third tantra teaches eightfold yoga — restraints, observances, postures, breath control, withdrawal, holding, meditation and absorption — and describes the eight powers (aṭṭamācitti) and other attainments that follow from it.
notes: Tantra-level reference.

paraphrase: The second tantra tells Śiva's great deeds and his five acts, and teaches that souls are of three classes — those with one mala, with two, and with three (vijñānākala, pralayākala, sakala).
notes: Tantra-level reference; placement of the three classes in tantra 2 moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The fourth tantra teaches mantras and diagrams (cakkaram), especially the diagram of the five letters of the sacred hall (tiruvampalac cakkaram), and the worship of the Goddess (Śakti) as Śiva's power.
notes: Tantra-level reference.

paraphrase: The ninth tantra sings the Dance (tirukkūttu) of Śiva in the hall of Tillai, which is also within the body and the heart, and the experience of Śiva beyond the tattvas.
notes: Tantra-level reference.

paraphrase: The first tantra teaches the guru's greatness, the impermanence of body, wealth and youth, and conduct: non-killing, not eating flesh, not coveting another's wife, not drinking, giving, learning and love.
notes: Tantra-level reference.

paraphrase: Campantar's first hymn: 'He with the ear-ring, riding the bull, crowned with the pure white moon, smeared with the ash of the burning ground — the thief who stole my heart' is the Lord of Brahmapuram (Cīkāḻi).
notes: Opening 'tōṭuṭaiya ceviyaṉ'; sung, by tradition, after Umā fed him the milk of knowledge.

paraphrase: The sacred ash (tirunīṟu) is mantra, is what the gods wear, is beauty, is praise, is the Āgama and the essence of Śaiva doctrine — the ash of the Lord of Tiruvālavāy (Madurai).
notes: Opening 'mantiramāvatu nīṟu'; by tradition sung to cure the Pāṇṭiya king's fever. Content of the listed epithets partly reconstructed.

paraphrase: For those who hold in their hearts the Lord who shares his body with Umā and who drank the poison, the planets and days are all auspicious — they do good, very good, to the Lord's devotees.
notes: The 'kōḷaṟu patikam', opening 'vēyuṟu tōḷipaṅkaṉ'.

paraphrase: May the brahmins, the gods and the cattle flourish; may cool rain fall; may the king prosper; may all evil sink; may the name of Hara resound and the world's suffering end.
notes: Opening 'vāḻka antaṇar'; by tradition the hymn written on the palm-leaf that floated upstream on the Vaikai in the contest with the Jains.

paraphrase: In most of Campantar's patikams the tenth verse denounces the Jains and Buddhists (their nakedness or robes, their denial of Śiva) and warns against their teaching; the eighth recalls Rāvaṇa crushed under Kailāsa and the ninth Brahmā and Viṣṇu failing to find Śiva's crown and feet.
notes: Structural teaching across Tirumuṟai 1–3; locator is a convention (books 1–3, verse 10).

paraphrase: Appar's first hymn at Tiruvatikai: 'I cannot tell what cruelties I have done; you do not ward off the pain that has come like death; it twists my bowels — I have worshipped you without cease; save me, Lord of Atikai Vīraṭṭāṉam.'
notes: Opening 'kūṟṟāyiṉavāṟu vilakkakilīr'; paraphrase partly reconstructed.

paraphrase: Even if they bind me to a stone and cast me into the sea, the good support that saves is 'namaccivāya' — the name of the Vedic Lord, the Light, whose feet are my refuge.
notes: Refrain 'kaṟṟuṇaip pūṭṭiyōr kaṭalil pāyccinum naṟṟuṇai yāvatu namaccivāyavē'; by tradition sung when thrown into the sea.

paraphrase: The shade of the twin feet of my Father, the Lord, is like a flawless vīṇā, the evening moon, the southern breeze, the swelling spring, and a pond humming with bees.
notes: Opening 'mācil vīṇaiyum mālai matiyamum'.

paraphrase: We are subject to no one; we do not fear Death; we will not suffer in hell; we know no deceit, no disease, and bow to none; we have joy always and no sorrow — for we are servants of Śaṅkara, who is no one's servant.
notes: Opening 'nāmārkkum kuṭiyallōm namaṉai añcōm'; by tradition his answer to the Pallava king's summons. Later lines paraphrased at moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Even if they give me the two celestial treasures with earth and heaven, I will not value them if they are not devotees of the Lord; but a leper, an outcaste who eats cow's flesh, if he is a servant of the Lord who bears the Gaṅgā, is the god we worship.
notes: Opening 'caṅkaniti patumaniti'; verse locator moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Cuntarar's first hymn: 'Madman (pittā), wearer of the crescent, great one, gracious one — how can I forget you, who took me as your own at Veṇṇeynallūr?'
notes: Opening 'pittā piṟaicūṭī'; sung when Śiva claimed him as his slave on his wedding day.

paraphrase: 'I am the servant of the servants of the brahmins who dwell in Tillai' — opening of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai, in which Cuntarar declares himself servant of each of Śiva's devotees by name.
notes: 'tillai vāḻ antaṇar tam aṭiyārkkum aṭiyēṉ'.

paraphrase: Praise to namaccivāya, praise to the feet of the Lord; praise to the feet of him who never leaves my heart even for the blink of an eye.

original.text: நமச்சிவாய வாஅழ்க நாதன்தாள் வாழ்க இமைப்பொழுதும் என்நெஞ்சில் நீங்காதான் தாள்வாழ்க

paraphrase: Born as grass, shrub, worm, tree, many beasts, bird, snake, stone, man, demon, spirit, asura, sage and god — in every moving and unmoving birth I have been born and am weary; today, seeing your golden feet, I am freed.
notes: 'pullāki pūṭāy puḻuvāy maramāki...'; line numbers approximate.

paraphrase: He is the one to whom the Vedas say 'not this, not this'; he came in grace as the guru, took me as his own, and cut my births.
notes: Reconstructed from the poem's themes; the exact wording and line not checked.

paraphrase: Tiruvaṇṭappakuti: the countless universes are like motes in a sunbeam before the Lord; he is inside and outside all, and he came to me, a mere dog, and made me his.
notes: Poem-level reference.

paraphrase: Tiruccatakam: the devotee weeps and melts, his hair stands on end, he dances and sings — yet laments that his heart has not melted enough; the melting of the heart is the sign of grace.
notes: Poem-level reference.

paraphrase: Tiruvempāvai: young women wake one another before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to bathe and sing Śiva's praise, and pray for husbands who are his devotees.
notes: Poem-level reference (20 verses).

paraphrase: Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci: the waking song, praising the Lord of Tirupperunturai at dawn as the gods throng to see him.
notes: Poem-level reference (10 verses).

paraphrase: Accappattu: I do not fear the snake in the anthill, nor the false ones' sweet words; I fear only those who do not think of the Lord who wears the crescent.
notes: Poem number and paraphrase moderate confidence.

paraphrase: From the day I was born and learned to speak, love for him grew; I came to his feet; he who dances with the dark throat — when will he end my sorrow?
notes: Paraphrase reconstructed; wording not checked.

paraphrase: The Lord dances at Tiruvālaṅkāṭu in the cremation ground at night among ghouls and jackals, with fire in his hand, while the ghoul-poet (the singer herself) watches and sings.
notes: Patikam-level reference.

paraphrase: The situations of love — meeting, union, separation, longing and marriage — set at Tillai, which the tradition reads as the soul's love for Śiva.
notes: Whole-work reference; the allegorical reading is the tradition's.

paraphrase: The opening word 'ulakelām' ('all the world'): the Lord whom all the world cannot know or tell, who dances in the hall, is praised.
notes: Tradition: the word was given by Śiva from the sky. Paraphrase of the rest of the verse moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The hunter Kaṇṇappar's worship with tasted meat, water from his mouth and flowers from his hair pleased Śiva more than the priest's correct rites; when the liṅga's eye bled he gave his own eye, and was stopped by Śiva from giving the second.
notes: Section-level locator (the purāṇam of Kaṇṇappar).

paraphrase: Nantaṉār, an outcaste, was admitted to Śiva's presence at Chidambaram after passing through fire at the Lord's command and rising as a sage.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār asked Śiva for undying love, no rebirth — or, if reborn, never to forget him — and to sing at his feet while he dances; he granted it.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: Ciṟuttoṇṭar and his wife gave even their only son to feed Śiva disguised as an ascetic, and the son was restored — teaching that nothing is withheld from a devotee of Śiva.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: The yogī from Kailāsa entered the body of the dead herdsman Mūlaṉ out of compassion for his cows, and, his own body taken away, stayed as Tirumūlar singing the Tirumantiram.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: Pūcalār built a temple in his mind, and Śiva chose to be present first at its consecration rather than at the king's temple of stone.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: The boy Caṇṭēcurar struck his father's feet when he kicked over the milk being offered to Śiva; Śiva made him chief of his servants.
notes: Section-level locator.

paraphrase: Appar left Jainism, was cured of colic by grace, survived the king's lime-kiln, poison, elephant and the sea by singing Śiva's names, and served by clearing grass from temple courtyards; offered gold and jewels by Śiva as a test, he threw them away as potsherds.
notes: Section-level locator; the gold episode moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Campantar, fed with the milk of knowledge by Umā at three, sang Śiva's hymns throughout the Tamil land, cured the Pāṇṭiya king with the sacred ash and defeated the Jains of Madurai in the fire and water ordeals.
notes: Section-level locator. The account continues with the Jains' impalement, which the tradition narrates; see the dispute record.

paraphrase: As the letter 'a' is the first of all letters, so the Primal Lord (Āti Pakavaṉ) is the first of the world.

original.text: அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம் ஆதி பகவன் முதற்றே உலகு

paraphrase: What is the use of learning, if one does not worship the good feet of the one of pure knowledge?

original.text: கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் வாலறிவன் நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்

paraphrase: Those who reach the glorious feet of the one who walked upon the flower (malarmicai ēkiṉāṉ) will live long on earth.
notes: Read by Jains as the Jina who walks on lotuses, by Śaivas as the Lord in the heart-lotus, by others as Brahmā/Viṣṇu or the Buddha.

paraphrase: The two deeds born of darkness (iruviṉai) do not cling to those who delight in the true praise of the Lord.
Those who stand in the flawless path of the one who destroyed the five gates of the senses (poṟivāyil aintavittāṉ) will live long.
Only those who reach the feet of the gracious one who is the ocean (or wheel) of virtue (aṟavāḻi antaṇaṉ) can cross the other seas.
Heads that do not bow to the feet of the one of eight qualities (eṇkuṇattāṉ) are like senses without function.
notes: Parimēlaḻakar glosses the eight qualities with Śiva's eight attributes from the Śaiva Āgamas; Jains read them as the eight qualities of a Siddha.

paraphrase: Those who reach the feet of the Lord cross the great ocean of births; others do not.

original.text: பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் நீந்தார் இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்

paraphrase: Indra, lord of the dwellers of the wide heaven, is witness to the power of one who has subdued the five senses.
To be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue; all else is empty display.

original.text: மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்தறன் ஆகுல நீர பிற

paraphrase: The loveless own everything for themselves; the loving belong to others even to their bones.

original.text: அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர் அன்புடையார் என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு

paraphrase: The body that love inhabits is the seat of life; in those without love it is bone wrapped in skin.
The whole purpose of keeping a household and living in it is to cherish guests and do good.
Not to kill and eat a living being is better than pouring ghee into the fire in a thousand sacrifices.
All living beings will join their hands in worship of one who neither kills nor eats flesh.

original.text: கொல்லான் புலாலை மறுத்தானைக் கைகூப்பி எல்லா உயிரும் தொழும்

paraphrase: As gold shines brighter the more it is burned, so the pain of austerity makes those who endure it shine.
Sharing one's food and protecting all living beings is the foremost of all precepts gathered by the authors of texts.

original.text: பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல் நூலோர் தொகுத்தவற்றுள் எல்லாம் தலை

paraphrase: Do not do what takes another's life, even if it costs you your own.
'He was here yesterday, he is not today' — such is the greatness of this world.
The bond between body and life is like a bird's that flies away leaving its shell (or nest) empty.
Death is like sleep; birth is like waking from sleep.

original.text: உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு உறங்கி விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு

paraphrase: One who destroys the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
Cling to the attachment of the One who is without attachment; cling to it so as to let go of attachment.

original.text: பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை அப்பற்றைப் பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு

paraphrase: Whatever a thing may appear to be, to see its true reality is wisdom.
Wisdom is to see the true reality called 'excellence' (ciṟappu, release), so that the folly called birth departs.
When desire, anger and delusion — even their names — are destroyed, suffering is destroyed.
Desire is the seed that yields, at every time and to every creature, unceasing birth.
If one gives up desire, never satisfied by its nature, that very state gives the unchanging nature.
What is stronger than fate (ūḻ)? Even when one devises another way, it comes first.
Learn thoroughly what is to be learned, and then live in accordance with it.

original.text: கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக

paraphrase: Whatever is heard from whomever, to discern its true meaning is wisdom.
The king free of sloth will gain all that was measured by the one who measured the worlds with his feet.
notes: An allusion to Viṣṇu as Trivikrama, cited by the Vaiṣṇava side.

paraphrase: Is the world of the lotus-eyed one sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the one you love?
notes: Cited by the Vaiṣṇava side (Viṣṇu's world).
